title: A Ruined Belt and a Warning
overview: Through a rotted belt, a saying about wineskins and stark poetry, Jeremiah warns Judah that its pride and worship of other gods will end in defeat and exile.

parts.label: The rotted belt (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: A linen belt worn snug around the waist pictures how closely the LORD had bound his people to himself, so they would bring him honor. Jeremiah hides it at Perath, most likely the Euphrates toward Babylon though some think a nearby place with a similar name, and when he digs it up it has rotted, a picture of a people spoiled by serving other gods.

parts.label: Every wineskin filled (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: Jeremiah quotes what sounds like an obvious saying, that every wineskin should be filled with wine, and the people shrug it off. He then turns it around: everyone from kings to priests will be filled with a staggering confusion like drunkenness and smashed against one another, and the text states the lack of pity bluntly.

parts.label: A last plea and tears (vv. 15-17)
parts.note: To give glory to God here means owning up before it is too late, pictured as travelers caught on mountain paths as night falls. If they refuse, Jeremiah says he will weep in private, because the people, the LORD's flock, will be taken captive.

parts.label: The king and his mother fall (vv. 18-19)
parts.note: These are most likely the young king Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, who held real power and were taken to Babylon in 597 BC. Even the towns of the far south will be cut off, and the whole of Judah will be carried away.

parts.label: Enemies from the north (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: The army coming from the north is Babylon, and the city is asked where its flock of people has gone. Verse 21 is hard to translate, but it seems to say Judah will be ruled by those it had treated as friends, and the city is pictured as a woman publicly stripped and abused, a harsh image of disgrace.

parts.label: A leopard's spots (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: A Cushite, someone from the upper Nile, cannot change his skin, nor a leopard its spots, and the point is that the people's wrongdoing had become just as fixed, not any judgment on skin color. So they will be scattered like chaff, and the shame image returns, with adultery standing for worship of other gods at hilltop shrines.

think: When a habit has become second nature, what do you think it actually takes to change it, if it can change at all?
